content.text: RH134: Red Hat Enterprise Linux 8 System Administration II
This chapter is different from the previous chapters. It does not introduce one new technology. It helps you review and combine the skills you learned throughout RH134.
The chapter contains three practical labs:
Fixing boot issues and maintaining servers.
Configuring and managing file systems and storage.
Configuring and managing server security.
The goal is to solve realistic administrator tasks without needing step-by-step instructions for every command.
Part 1: Review of the RH134 Course
Part 2: Lab 1 — Fixing Boot Issues and Maintaining Servers
Part 3: Lab 2 — Configuring and Managing File Systems and Storage
Main idea: Use shell features and commands to perform tasks more efficiently.
Simple explanation: Instead of typing the same command many times, Linux lets you automate repeated work with shell scripts, loops, conditions, and text-search tools.
Example:
What each part means:
for: Starts a loop.
user: A variable that holds one value at a time.
in: Introduces the list of values.
do and done: Mark the beginning and end of the loop's work.
echo: Displays the current value.
$user: Reads the variable's value.
This displays each name on a separate line.
Remember: Loops and scripts let you automate repeated command-line work.
Main idea: Linux can run commands once in the future or repeatedly on a schedule.
Simple explanation: Imagine setting an alarm. You decide when the task should run, and Linux runs it without you manually entering the command at that time.
The course covers at, cron, and systemd timers.
Example:
What each part means:
crontab: Manages a user's scheduled jobs.
-l: Lists the current user's scheduled jobs.
A cron job might run a backup every weekday evening.
Remember: Use at for a one-time scheduled task, cron for recurring schedules, and systemd timers for timer-based service tasks.
Main idea: Linux provides tools for selecting performance profiles and adjusting process priority.
Simple explanation: A computer may run many programs at once. You can influence how much attention the CPU gives to individual processes and select a tuning profile appropriate for the system.
Example:
What each part means:
nice: Starts a command with a chosen scheduling priority.
-n 10: Sets the nice value to 10.
command: Placeholder for the program you want to run.
A higher nice value generally means a lower scheduling priority. The value does not directly specify a percentage of CPU usage.
Remember: nice starts a process with a priority setting; renice changes the priority of a running process.
Main idea: ACLs let you give specific users or groups permissions beyond the basic owner/group/other permissions.
Simple explanation: Basic Linux permissions provide three broad categories: owner, group, and others. ACLs let you make more specific exceptions.
Example:
What each part means:
setfacl: Changes ACL permissions.
-m: Modifies or adds an ACL entry.
u:alice:rw: Gives user alice read (r) and write (w) permission.
report.txt: The file being changed.
To inspect ACLs:
Default ACLs on a directory can influence permissions on new files and subdirectories created inside it.
Remember: Use ACLs when ordinary owner, group, and other permissions are not flexible enough.
Main idea: SELinux applies additional rules that control how processes access system resources.
Simple explanation: Traditional file permissions are like a key to a room. SELinux is another security check that decides whether a particular process is allowed to perform an action there.
Example:
Possible output:
This shows that SELinux is enforcing its policy.
The course also covers SELinux contexts, Booleans, and investigating denials in audit logs.
Remember: Do not disable SELinux just because an application fails; inspect the denial and correct the underlying configuration when possible.
Main idea: Linux can partition disks, create file systems, mount storage, and use swap space.
Simple explanation: A disk is storage hardware. A partition divides it into sections. A file system organizes data in a section, and mounting makes that file system accessible through a directory.
Example:
What each part means:
- lsblk: Lists block devices such as disks, partitions, and logical volumes.
To use a newly prepared file system, you typically create it with a formatting tool and mount it. Formatting the wrong device can destroy data, so always verify the target first.
Remember: A disk, partition, file system, and mount point are different parts of the storage process.
Main idea: Linux offers storage-management tools that make storage easier to allocate and maintain.
Simple explanation:
LVM: Combines storage into flexible volume groups and creates logical volumes from them.
Stratis: Provides a higher-level way to manage local storage pools and file systems.
VDO: Can reduce the physical storage used for data through techniques such as compression and deduplication.
Example:
These commands display LVM physical volumes, volume groups, and logical volumes.
What each part means:
pvs: Shows physical volumes.
vgs: Shows volume groups.
lvs: Shows logical volumes.
Remember: LVM, Stratis, and VDO solve related but different storage-management problems.
Main idea: Linux can access storage provided by another computer across a network.
Simple explanation: Instead of keeping all files on the local disk, a server can access a shared directory hosted by another system.
NFS is a common protocol for sharing directories between Linux and Unix systems. The course also covers automatic mounting with autofs.
Example:
What each part means:
mount: Attaches a file system to a directory.
servera:/share: The NFS server and exported directory.
/local-share: The local directory where the share becomes accessible.
For persistent mounting, configure /etc/fstab or an appropriate automounter map.
Remember: NFS provides remote file access; /etc/fstab and autofs help control when the share is mounted.

Main idea: The last two chapters covered firewall rules, SELinux port labels, RHEL installation, Kickstart, and virtualization.

Simple explanation: A working network service needs more than an application that starts successfully. Its configuration must permit the required network access, and security policy must allow it to operate.
Similarly, installing a server manually is different from automating many installations with Kickstart or running a separate operating system in a virtual machine.

Remember: Troubleshoot each layer separately and use the correct installation method for the task.

sections.title: 13. Remount the root file system as writable

content.text: Main idea: Emergency mode may mount the root file system as read-only, so you may need to remount it before editing configuration files.
Simple explanation: Read-only means you can inspect files but cannot change them. To repair /etc/fstab, the root file system must be writable.
Example:
What each part means:
mount: Manages mounted file systems.
-o: Supplies mount options.
remount: Changes options on an already mounted file system.
rw: Read-write mode.
/: The root file system.
Next, check all file systems listed in /etc/fstab:
In this lab, the command reports a mount failure involving a fake UUID and /FakeMount.
Remember: Use mount -a to test the file-system entries, but inspect the error before editing anything.

sections.title: 18. Create a partition and LVM logical volume

content.text: Main idea: LVM builds flexible logical storage on top of physical storage devices or partitions.
The book uses the unpartitioned disk /dev/vdb.
Create a partition table and a 2 GiB partition:
What each part means:
parted: Manages disk partitions.
/dev/vdb: The target disk.
mklabel msdos: Creates an MBR-style partition table.
mkpart primary 1GiB 3GiB: Creates a partition between the specified positions.
Warning: mklabel replaces the existing partition table. Use it only on the intended lab disk.
Create an LVM physical volume:
Create the volume group:
Create the logical volume:
What each part means:
pvcreate: Prepares the partition for LVM.
vgcreate: Creates the volume group.
lvcreate: Creates a logical volume.
-L 1GiB: Requests a 1 GiB size.
-n vol_home: Sets the logical volume's name.
extra_storage: The volume group from which space is allocated.
Remember: LVM follows the structure physical volume → volume group → logical volume.
